lesson.title: Writing It Right: The Independence Setup
lesson.summary: Setup for an independence test turns on confirming a single sample with two measured variables and writing hypotheses about association, a subtly different template from homogeneity's same distribution across groups language.
lesson.body:
Just as with homogeneity, the hardest part of a test for independence is often not the arithmetic but the setup: confirming the sampling structure and writing the hypotheses correctly.

Start by confirming the structure. An independence test needs exactly one random sample from one population, with two categorical variables measured on every individual in that sample. This is the key difference from homogeneity's setup: homogeneity begins with several separate samples and one variable, independence begins with one sample and two variables. In the exercise and sleep example, there is a single sample of 200 adults, and exercise frequency and sleep quality are both recorded for each of them, which is exactly the independence structure.

With the two variables identified, write the hypotheses using independence's specific template:

H0: There is no association between variable 1 and variable 2 in the population, equivalently, the two variables are independent.
Ha: There is an association between variable 1 and variable 2 in the population, equivalently, the two variables are not independent.

Applied to the example: H0 is that there is no association between exercise frequency and sleep quality among adults in this population. Ha is that there is an association between exercise frequency and sleep quality among adults in this population.

Watch for the same kind of language mix-up flagged in the homogeneity setup chapter, but in reverse. Writing H0 as the distribution of sleep quality is the same across exercise groups borrows homogeneity's phrasing for a situation that does not have separately sampled groups at all, only one sample sorted two ways after the fact. It happens to be numerically equivalent, since independence and homogeneity share the exact same expected count formula and chi-square arithmetic, but the wording should match how the data were actually collected: a single population studied on two variables calls for association or independence language, not same distribution across groups language.

Setup also requires checking the same three conditions from earlier in this unit: random, the 200 adults form one random sample, independent, individual responses independent of one another and the sample of 200 no more than 10% of the full adult population being studied, which is virtually always true for a population that large, and large counts, every expected count at least 5, confirmed in the previous chapter with a minimum of 27. With the structure, hypotheses, and conditions all confirmed, the calculation from the previous chapter can be trusted to produce a valid P-value.
